newsitem.title: CANADA: OECD says Canada's high unemployment could linger.
newsitem.headline: OECD says Canada's high unemployment could linger.

text.p: Canada's high unemployment rate is poised for only a slow decline despite the country's favorable economic growth prospects over the medium term, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development said on Wednesday.

The OECD, in its annual report on the Canadian economy, suggested that the pace of economic expansion would gain momentum over the next 18 months, backed by strong export growth and increasing domestic demand.

"With stronger growth in the United States boosting exports and the substantial fall in Canadian interest rates that has taken place over the past year having an increasing impact on domestic demand, the pace of economic expansion is projected to gather momentum," the OECD report said.
But stronger economic growth would bring only a gradual decline in the unemployment rate, which the OECD projected to average 8.7 percent for the period between 1996 and 2002.
Canada's unemployment stood at 10.0 percent in October.
The organization projected real gross domestic product (GDP) to average 3.2 percent for the same period, compared to 1.4 percent for the 1988-1995 period.

Canada's strong trade performance should ensure that the country's external current account moved close to balance, while the persistent slack in its product and labor markets would keep inflation in the lower half of the Bank of Canada's 1.0 to 3.0 percent target range.
But the OECD said that the period of slow economic growth in Canada could last longer than expected, as consumer confidence remained low and household debt levels were high.
"An additional risk is that the contraction in public spending that is under way could have a larger adverse effect on near-term activity than assumed," the OECD report said.
The organization praised the recent aggressive monetary easing by the Bank of Canada, which has brought short-term interest rates well below their U.S. equivalents.

"Continued efforts to make monetary policy more transparent would further strengthen the effectiveness of the inflation-target framework in place, thereby limiting the risk that any policy moves would induce adverse reactions in financial markets," the OECD report said.
The organization also warned both the federal and provincial governments to continue cutting their deficits in order to keep investor confidence and maintain the credibility of their fiscal planning.

Reducing spending, rather than increasing revenues, should continue to be the focus of fiscal consolidation, the OECD said, noting that maintaining the same degree of fiscal restraint may become increasingly difficult as federal program spending had reached historically low levels and pressures were mounting to ease the tax burden on Canadians.
"Given the magnitude of outstanding debt, there is no scope for easing fiscal retrenchment efforts," the OECD said.

It noted that even if the federal government's current budget targets are met, Canada's net public debt-to-GDP ratio will start falling only in 1997 and it may be a while before it comes close to the OECD average.
